title: ThunderNet: Towards Real-time Generic Object Detection

problem.summary: Real-time detection on mobile devices is hard: modern detectors are resource-hungry, lightweight one-stage detectors are the default route to speed but leave a large accuracy gap and still are not real time on mobile, while naively pairing a small backbone with a heavy two-stage detection part creates imbalance, redundancy and overfitting.
statements: Mobile devices are computation-constrained while modern CNN detectors are resource-hungry and require massive computation for ideal accuracy.
Lightweight one-stage detectors have a huge accuracy gap to large detectors and fail to run in real time on mobile devices.
One-stage detectors skip RoI-wise feature extraction, so their results are coarser than two-stage detectors, and the problem is worse for lightweight models.
Classification backbones transferred to detection lack the receptive field and low-level features detection needs, obstructing further compression.
A light detection head coupled with a small backbone induces imbalance between backbone and detection part, causing redundancy and overfitting.

evidence.quote: However, modern CNN-based detectors are resource-hungry and require massive computation to achieve ideal detection accuracy, which hinders them from real-time inference in mobile scenarios.

Prior lightweight one-stage detectors [11, 28, 31, 13] do not obtain an ideal accuracy/speed trade-off: there is a huge accuracy gap between them and the large detectors [19, 25], while they fail to achieve real-time detection on mobile devices.
However, as one-stage detectors do not conduct RoI-wise feature extraction and recognition, their results are coarser than two-stage detectors. The problem is aggravated for lightweight detectors.
The gap between the two tasks restricts the performance of these backbones on object detection and obstructs further compression without harming detection accuracy.

background.summary: ThunderNet builds on two-stage detection (Faster R-CNN RPN, R-FCN, Light-Head R-CNN), on FPN feature pyramids, and on lightweight classification backbones (ShuffleNetV2, MobileNet, Xception); the claimed gaps are that transferred classification backbones are suboptimal for detection, specialized detection backbones are still under-studied, and no prior work had shown two-stage detectors effective for real-time detection.

relatedWork.name: Light-Head R-CNN
relatedWork.quote: LightHead R-CNN [14] adopts a lightweight detection head and achieves real-time detection on GPU.

relatedWork.name: DetNet
relatedWork.relation: prior example of a backbone designed specifically for detection
relatedWork.quote: DetNet [15] designs a backbone specifically for object detection.

relatedWork.name: FPN
relatedWork.relation: prior multi-scale context mechanism that is too costly here
relatedWork.quote: FPN [16] exploits the inherent multi-scale, pyramidal hierarchy of CNNs to construct feature pyramids.

relatedWork.name: MobileNet-SSD / Pelee / Tiny-DSOD
relatedWork.relation: prior lightweight one-stage detectors used as baselines
relatedWork.quote: lightweight one-stage detectors, such as MobileNet-SSD [11], MobileNetV2-SSDLite [28], Pelee [31] and Tiny-DSOD [13], achieve inference on mobile devices at low frame rates.

evidence.quote: However, image classification and object detection require different properties of networks. Therefore, simply transferring classification networks to object detection is not optimal.
Commonly, one-stage detectors are regarded as the key to real-time detection.
This imbalance not only induces great redundancy but makes the network prone to overfitting.

solution.summary: ThunderNet is a lightweight two-stage detector built from an SNet backbone (ShuffleNetV2 with 5x5 depthwise convolutions and strengthened early stages), a compressed RPN and a narrowed Light-Head R-CNN head with PSRoI align, plus two cheap blocks: a Context Enhancement Module fusing C4/C5/global context and a Spatial Attention Module that reweights features using RPN knowledge, all at 320x320 input.
solution.approach: Pair a detection-specific lightweight SNet backbone with a compressed two-stage head, and restore context and foreground/background feature separation with the cheap CEM and SAM blocks.
components: SNet49 / SNet146 / SNet535 backbones based on ShuffleNetV2 with 5x5 depthwise convolutions and expanded early-stage channels
compressed RPN: 5x5 depthwise convolution followed by a 256-channel 1x1 convolution
narrowed thin feature map (alpha halved to 5) with PSRoI align and a 1024-d fc R-CNN subnet
Context Enhancement Module merging C4, C5 and globally pooled context at 245 channels
Spatial Attention Module: F_SAM = F_CEM * sigmoid(theta(F_RPN))
320x320 input resolution matched to backbone capacity
multi-scale training over {240, 320, 480} pixels with heavy augmentation, OHEM, Soft-NMS and Cross-GPU Batch Normalization

evidence.quote: we propose a lightweight two-stage generic object detector named ThunderNet.
We present three SNet backbones: SNet49 for faster inference, SNet535 for better accuracy, and SNet146 for a better speed/accuracy trade-off.
The key idea of CEM is to aggregate multi-scale local context information and global context information to generate more discriminative features.
The key idea of SAM is to use the knowledge from RPN to refine the feature distribution of the feature map.
F SAM = F CEM · sigmoid(θ(F RPN )).

experiments.summary: ThunderNet is trained end-to-end with synchronized SGD and evaluated on PASCAL VOC 2007 test and COCO test-dev against lightweight one-stage detectors and larger detectors, with ablations over input resolution, backbone design, RPN/head compression, CEM and SAM, and separate ARM/CPU/GPU speed measurements.

benchmarks.split: Xeon E5-2682v4 CPU, single thread, SNet49

evidence.quote: ThunderNet surpasses previous lightweight one-stage detectors with only 40% of the computational cost on PASCAL VOC and COCO benchmarks.
Without bells and whistles, ThunderNet runs at 24.1 fps on an ARM-based device with 19.2 AP on COCO.
ThunderNet with SNet146 surpasses MobileNet-SSD [11], MobileNet-SSDLite [28], and Pelee [31] with less than 40% of the computational cost.
ThunderNet with SNet49 outperforms MobileNet-SSD with merely 21% of the FLOPs, while the SNet146-based model surpasses Tiny-DSOD by 2.9 mAP with about 43% of the FLOPs.

limitations.summary: Absolute accuracy is still far below large detectors (best 28.1 AP on COCO), AP50 trails Tiny-DSOD because of its deep supervision and feature pyramid, the small 320x320 input loses detail, and SNet's ImageNet classification accuracy is lower than the ShuffleNetV2 baselines it starts from.
items: Best COCO result is 28.1 AP (SNet535, 1300 MFLOPs), and the cheapest variant SNet49 only reaches MobileNet-SSD level accuracy (19.2 AP).
Compared with Tiny-DSOD, ThunderNet has better AP but worse AP50; the authors attribute the classification gap to Tiny-DSOD's deep supervision and feature pyramid.
Small input resolution causes low-resolution feature maps and loss of detail features that backbone capacity alone cannot fix.
SNet146 has lower ImageNet top-1 accuracy than ShuffleNetV2 (32.5 vs 31.4 top-1 error) even though detection is better.

evidence.quote: Compared with Tiny-DSOD [13], ThunderNet achieves better AP but worse AP50 with 42% of the FLOPs.
SNet146 achieves better detection results though the classification accuracy is lower.
It is hard to be remedied by simply increasing the capacity of the backbones.

applications.detail: The method targets real-time generic detection on mobile platforms and is benchmarked on a Snapdragon 845 ARM CPU, x86 CPU and a GeForce 1080Ti GPU.
applications.quote: Real-time generic object detection on mobile platforms is a crucial but challenging computer vision task.

applications.detail: The work was done in collaboration with Megvii Inc., with one author interning there.
applications.quote: This work was done when Zheng Qin was an intern at Megvii Inc.

deploymentClaims: 24.1 fps single-thread on Snapdragon 845 (ARM) and 47.3 fps on Xeon E5-2682v4 CPU with SNet49
All three model variants run at over 200 fps on a GeForce 1080Ti GPU
Batch normalization layers are merged with preceding convolutions for faster inference
Code and models released at github.com/qinzheng93/ThunderNet

evidence.quote: ThunderNet with SNet49 achieves real-time detection on both ARM and CPU at 24.1 and 47.3 fps, respectively.
These results suggest that ThunderNet is highly efficient in real-world applications.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-time detector and the fastest single-thread speed on ARM platforms ever reported.
